claim: Thermal injury impairs sensory axon regeneration in larval zebrafish.
source: Here, we found that thermal but not mechanical injury impairs sensory axon regeneration and function.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced axon density and impaired touch responsiveness in burned larvae compared to transected larvae.

claim: Mechanical injury does not impair sensory axon regeneration in larval zebrafish.
source: Here, we found that thermal but not mechanical injury impairs sensory axon regeneration and function.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing normal axon density and touch responsiveness in transected larvae.

claim: Thermal injury impairs sensory neuron function in larval zebrafish.
source: Here, we found that thermal but not mechanical injury impairs sensory axon regeneration and function.
evidence: Supported by touch assay data showing lack of touch responsiveness in burned larvae.

claim: Thermal injury triggers rapid Arp2/3-dependent migration of keratinocytes.
source: Real-time imaging revealed an immediate tissue response to thermal injury characterized by the rapid Arp2/3-dependent migration of keratinocytes, which was associated with tissue scale ROS production and sustained sensory axon damage.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data and CK666 inhibition experiments showing Arp2/3-dependent keratinocyte migration.

claim: Rapid keratinocyte migration after thermal injury is associated with tissue scale ROS production.
source: Real-time imaging revealed an immediate tissue response to thermal injury characterized by the rapid Arp2/3-dependent migration of keratinocytes, which was associated with tissue scale ROS production and sustained sensory axon damage.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf fluorescence measurements showing elevated ROS throughout the fin tissue after burn injury.

claim: Rapid keratinocyte migration after thermal injury is associated with sustained sensory axon damage.
source: Real-time imaging revealed an immediate tissue response to thermal injury characterized by the rapid Arp2/3-dependent migration of keratinocytes, which was associated with tissue scale ROS production and sustained sensory axon damage.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging showing prolonged axonal damage extending beyond the initial wound area.

claim: Isotonic treatment limits keratinocyte movement after burn injury.
source: Isotonic treatment was sufficient to limit keratinocyte movement, spatially restrict ROS production, and rescue sensory neuron function.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data showing reduced keratinocyte speed and distance in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Isotonic treatment spatially restricts ROS production after burn injury.
source: Isotonic treatment was sufficient to limit keratinocyte movement, spatially restrict ROS production, and rescue sensory neuron function.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements showing ROS localized to wound edge in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Isotonic treatment rescues sensory neuron function after burn injury.
source: Isotonic treatment was sufficient to limit keratinocyte movement, spatially restrict ROS production, and rescue sensory neuron function.
evidence: Supported by touch assay data showing >85% of isotonic-treated larvae had normal sensory function at 24 hpw.

claim: Early keratinocyte dynamics regulate the spatial and temporal pattern of long-term signaling in the wound microenvironment during tissue repair.
source: These results suggest that early keratinocyte dynamics regulate the spatial and temporal pattern of long-term signaling in the wound microenvironment during tissue repair.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that early keratinocyte migration affects ROS distribution and sensory neuron outcomes.

claim: Peripheral sensory neurons innervate the skin.
source: Restoration of tissue function following epithelial injury requires the regeneration and activity of peripheral sensory neurons, which innervate the skin (Mullen et al., 1996; Rabiller et al., 2021; Simões et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Restoration of tissue function following epithelial injury requires the regeneration and activity of peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Restoration of tissue function following epithelial injury requires the regeneration and activity of peripheral sensory neurons, which innervate the skin (Mullen et al., 1996; Rabiller et al., 2021; Simões et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Axonal regeneration requires the clearance of axon fragments by phagocytes followed by new axonal growth.
source: In response to tissue damage, axonal regeneration requires the clearance of axon fragments by phagocytes followed by new axonal growth (Rasmussen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Peripheral sensory neurons maintain a cell-intrinsic ability to regenerate following injury.
source: While peripheral sensory neurons maintain a cell-intrinsic ability to regenerate following injury (Liu et al., 2011; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Renthal et al., 2020), local environmental cues also regulate the response of sensory neurons to tissue damage in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Local environmental cues regulate the response of sensory neurons to tissue damage in vivo.
source: While peripheral sensory neurons maintain a cell-intrinsic ability to regenerate following injury (Liu et al., 2011; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Renthal et al., 2020), local environmental cues also regulate the response of sensory neurons to tissue damage in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and the experimental findings in this manuscript.

claim: Supporting cell populations contribute to peripheral sensory axon regeneration.
source: Recent advances have identified the contribution of supporting cell populations, paracrine biochemical signaling, and biophysical interactions in regulating peripheral sensory axon regeneration (Avraham et al., 2021; Cheah et al., 2017; Villegas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Paracrine biochemical signaling contributes to peripheral sensory axon regeneration.
source: Recent advances have identified the contribution of supporting cell populations, paracrine biochemical signaling, and biophysical interactions in regulating peripheral sensory axon regeneration (Avraham et al., 2021; Cheah et al., 2017; Villegas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biophysical interactions contribute to peripheral sensory axon regeneration.
source: Recent advances have identified the contribution of supporting cell populations, paracrine biochemical signaling, and biophysical interactions in regulating peripheral sensory axon regeneration (Avraham et al., 2021; Cheah et al., 2017; Villegas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Keratinocytes are a primary constituent of epithelial tissue.
source: Keratinocytes are a primary constituent of epithelial tissue and play a critical role in wound healing.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about tissue composition.

claim: Keratinocytes play a critical role in wound healing.
source: Keratinocytes are a primary constituent of epithelial tissue and play a critical role in wound healing.
evidence: Supported by the experimental findings and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Keratinocytes mediate wound closure by actively migrating toward the site of injury.
source: In addition to mediating wound closure by actively migrating toward the site of injury, keratinocytes also generate pro-reparative signals such as reactive oxygen species (ROS), which coordinate longer-term repair pathways (Dunnill et al., 2017; Linley et al., 2012; Love et al., 2013; Mittal et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2018; Sies and Jones, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Keratinocytes generate pro-reparative signals such as reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: In addition to mediating wound closure by actively migrating toward the site of injury, keratinocytes also generate pro-reparative signals such as reactive oxygen species (ROS), which coordinate longer-term repair pathways (Dunnill et al., 2017; Linley et al., 2012; Love et al., 2013; Mittal et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2018; Sies and Jones, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ROS coordinate longer-term repair pathways.
source: In addition to mediating wound closure by actively migrating toward the site of injury, keratinocytes also generate pro-reparative signals such as reactive oxygen species (ROS), which coordinate longer-term repair pathways (Dunnill et al., 2017; Linley et al., 2012; Love et al., 2013; Mittal et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2018; Sies and Jones, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transient and localized ROS production promotes regeneration and sensory axon regrowth.
source: While transient and localized ROS production promotes regeneration and sensory axon regrowth, chronically elevated ROS is associated with neurodegeneration and disease (Cobb and Cole, 2015; Rieger and Sagasti, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chronically elevated ROS is associated with neurodegeneration and disease.
source: While transient and localized ROS production promotes regeneration and sensory axon regrowth, chronically elevated ROS is associated with neurodegeneration and disease (Cobb and Cole, 2015; Rieger and Sagasti, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Precise temporal and spatial organization of tissue redox signaling is critical for efficient sensory neuron regeneration and tissue repair.
source: Thus, precise temporal and spatial organization of tissue redox signaling is likely critical for efficient sensory neuron regeneration and tissue repair.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting effects of transient vs. chronic ROS and supported by experimental findings.

claim: Burn wounds heal poorly.
source: While epithelial tissue is well adapted to repair from mechanical damage, burn wounds heal poorly.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge and supported by experimental findings.

claim: Thermal injury results in chronic pain in affected tissue.
source: Thermal injury results in chronic pain and lack of sensation in the affected tissue, suggesting that an abnormal sensory neuron response contributes to burn wound pathophysiology (Blais et al., 2013; Choinière et al., 1991; Pavoni et al., 2010; Tirado-Esteban et al., 2020; Tsolakidis et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Thermal injury results in lack of sensation in affected tissue.
source: Thermal injury results in chronic pain and lack of sensation in the affected tissue, suggesting that an abnormal sensory neuron response contributes to burn wound pathophysiology (Blais et al., 2013; Choinière et al., 1991; Pavoni et al., 2010; Tirado-Esteban et al., 2020; Tsolakidis et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An abnormal sensory neuron response contributes to burn wound pathophysiology.
source: Thermal injury results in chronic pain and lack of sensation in the affected tissue, suggesting that an abnormal sensory neuron response contributes to burn wound pathophysiology (Blais et al., 2013; Choinière et al., 1991; Pavoni et al., 2010; Tirado-Esteban et al., 2020; Tsolakidis et al., 2022).
evidence: Inferred from clinical observations cited in prior literature.

claim: Thermal injury in larval zebrafish results in persistent inflammation.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated persistent inflammation and a loss of an organized collagen matrix that impairs healing after thermal injury in larval zebrafish (LeBert et al., 2018; LeBert et al., 2015; Miskolci et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Thermal injury in larval zebrafish results in loss of an organized collagen matrix that impairs healing.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated persistent inflammation and a loss of an organized collagen matrix that impairs healing after thermal injury in larval zebrafish (LeBert et al., 2018; LeBert et al., 2015; Miskolci et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Larval zebrafish thermal injury features recapitulate human burns.
source: These features recapitulate human burns and provide an in vivo model system to study the regeneration of sensory neurons in the wound microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of zebrafish and human burn characteristics.

claim: Larval zebrafish provide an in vivo model system to study the regeneration of sensory neurons in the wound microenvironment.
source: These features recapitulate human burns and provide an in vivo model system to study the regeneration of sensory neurons in the wound microenvironment.
evidence: Based on the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: Localized thermal injury induces axonal damage in the tailfin of larval zebrafish.
source: We found that localized thermal injury induced axonal damage in the tailfin.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data showing calcium-positive punctae in axons.

claim: Sensory axons are physically displaced following burn injury.
source: Live imaging revealed that sensory axons are physically displaced and experience damage associated with the rapid collective migration of basal keratinocytes following burn.
evidence: Supported by dual-labeled imaging showing coordinated movement of axons and keratinocytes.

claim: Sensory axons experience damage associated with the rapid collective migration of basal keratinocytes following burn.
source: Live imaging revealed that sensory axons are physically displaced and experience damage associated with the rapid collective migration of basal keratinocytes following burn.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging showing axonal damage coinciding with keratinocyte migration.

claim: Early keratinocyte migration contributes to elevated ROS at the tissue scale after burn injury.
source: This early keratinocyte migration also contributes to elevated ROS at the tissue scale.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements showing reduced tissue-scale ROS when keratinocyte migration is inhibited.

claim: Keratinocyte migration after burn injury is dependent on Arp2/3 signaling.
source: Keratinocyte migration was dependent on Arp2/3 signaling and treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 dampened early wound-localized ROS production after burn, suggesting that dysregulated migration perturbs the temporal and spatial organization of ROS after tissue damage.
evidence: Supported by CK666 treatment experiments showing reduced keratinocyte migration and altered ROS distribution.

claim: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 dampens early wound-localized ROS production after burn.
source: Keratinocyte migration was dependent on Arp2/3 signaling and treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 dampened early wound-localized ROS production after burn, suggesting that dysregulated migration perturbs the temporal and spatial organization of ROS after tissue damage.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements in CK666-treated larvae.

claim: Dysregulated migration perturbs the temporal and spatial organization of ROS after tissue damage.
source: Keratinocyte migration was dependent on Arp2/3 signaling and treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 dampened early wound-localized ROS production after burn, suggesting that dysregulated migration perturbs the temporal and spatial organization of ROS after tissue damage.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that inhibiting migration alters ROS distribution.

claim: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution spatially restricts ROS production after burn injury.
source: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution spatially restricted ROS production and rescued sensory axon regrowth and function.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements showing ROS localized to wound edge in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution rescues sensory axon regrowth after burn injury.
source: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution spatially restricted ROS production and rescued sensory axon regrowth and function.
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements showing improved regeneration in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution rescues sensory axon function after burn injury.
source: Inhibiting keratinocyte migration via osmotic manipulation with isotonic solution spatially restricted ROS production and rescued sensory axon regrowth and function.
evidence: Supported by touch assay data showing restored sensory function in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Regulated keratinocyte behavior is important for early temporal and spatial signal control that leads to sensory axon regeneration and tissue repair.
source: Collectively, our results support the importance of regulated keratinocyte behavior for early temporal and spatial signal control that leads to sensory axon regeneration and tissue repair.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental findings showing that modulating keratinocyte migration affects ROS distribution and sensory neuron outcomes.

claim: Burned larvae had significantly reduced sensory axon density at 24 hours post-wound compared to uninjured fins.
source: In contrast, we found that burned larvae had significantly reduced sensory axon density, with an axon density of 63.7±0.02% compared to uninjured fins (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Axon density in burned larvae was 63.7±0.02% of uninjured fins at 24 hours post-wound.
source: In contrast, we found that burned larvae had significantly reduced sensory axon density, with an axon density of 63.7±0.02% compared to uninjured fins (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The relative decrease in axon density after burn injury was sustained even 96 hours post-wound.
source: This relative decrease was sustained even 96 hpw with an axon density of only 65.1±0.04% compared to control (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Axon density in burned larvae was 65.1±0.04% of control at 96 hours post-wound.
source: This relative decrease was sustained even 96 hpw with an axon density of only 65.1±0.04% compared to control (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Following transection, axon density was 89.5±0.02% of the density observed in age-matched uninjured larvae 24 hours post-wound.
source: Following transection, axon density was 89.5±0.02% of the density observed in age-matched uninjured larvae 24 hpw.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of axon density.

claim: Larvae wounded by transection had a nearly 100% response rate to touch at 24 hours post-wound.
source: As expected, larvae wounded by transection had a nearly 100% response rate 24 hpw, indicating the rapid recovery of sensory neurons following mechanical injury (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: None of the burned larvae were sensitive to touch at 24 hours post-wound.
source: In contrast, none of the burned larvae were sensitive to touch 24 hpw with resolution occurring by 96 hpw (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sensory function in burned larvae resolves by 96 hours post-wound.
source: In contrast, none of the burned larvae were sensitive to touch 24 hpw with resolution occurring by 96 hpw (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All tested larvae exhibited a tail flick reflex when pressure was applied to the trunk.
source: Importantly, all tested larvae exhibited a tail flick reflex when pressure was applied to the trunk, showing that the impaired sensation was limited to the damaged tissue.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data.

claim: The impaired sensation after burn injury was limited to the damaged tissue.
source: Importantly, all tested larvae exhibited a tail flick reflex when pressure was applied to the trunk, showing that the impaired sensation was limited to the damaged tissue.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that larvae responded to trunk stimulation but not wound stimulation.

claim: GCaMP can be used for real-time labeling of axon damage in larval zebrafish.
source: Therefore, GCaMP can be used for real-time labeling of axon damage in larval zebrafish (Adalbert et al., 2012; Linsley et al., 2021; Ziv and Spira, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and experimental validation in this study.

claim: Axon damage is characterized by the fragmenting of axons and the formation of small punctae.
source: Axon damage is characterized by the fragmenting of axons and the formation of small punctae, which are later cleared by phagocytes (Reyes et al., 2004; Villegas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Axon fragments are later cleared by phagocytes.
source: Axon damage is characterized by the fragmenting of axons and the formation of small punctae, which are later cleared by phagocytes (Reyes et al., 2004; Villegas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The neurotoxin sodium azide elicits widespread and long-lasting calcium-positive punctae in sensory neurons.
source: Accordingly, the neurotoxin sodium azide elicited widespread and long-lasting calcium-positive punctae, indicating sustained axonal damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Linsley et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Elavl3 promoter is expressed by both sensory and motor neurons.
source: Unlike Ngn1, the Elavl3 promoter is expressed by both sensory and motor neurons.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of promoter expression patterns.

claim: Ngn1 depleted larvae lack responsiveness to touch stimulation.
source: These larvae did not have any obvious developmental defects but lacked responsiveness to touch stimulation, as previously reported (Cornell and Eisen, 2002).
evidence: Supported by behavioral assay data and citation to prior literature.

claim: No calcium increase was detected in Ngn1 depleted larvae following injury.
source: As expected, no calcium increase was detected in Ngn1 depleted larvae following injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tailfin transection results in spatially localized axonal damage that is almost completely resolved by 1 hour post-wound.
source: In agreement with previous observations of axonal damage following mechanical injury (Arrázola et al., 2019; Rasmussen et al., 2015; Rieger and Sagasti, 2011), tailfin transection resulted in spatially localized axonal damage that was almost completely resolved by 1 hpw (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 1E and citations to prior literature.

claim: Burn injury results in a distinct temporal and spatial profile of sensory axon damage compared to transection.
source: In contrast, burn injury resulted in a distinct temporal and spatial profile of sensory axon damage.
evidence: Supported by comparative GCaMP5 imaging data between burn and transection injuries.

claim: Initial wound-induced sensory neuron-specific calcium increase after burn appears to be localized to burned tissue.
source: While initial wound-induced sensory neuron-specific calcium increase appeared to be localized to burned tissue, axonal damage continued to increase and spread across the tissue for approximately 6 hr (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Axonal damage after burn injury continues to increase and spread across the tissue for approximately 6 hours.
source: While initial wound-induced sensory neuron-specific calcium increase appeared to be localized to burned tissue, axonal damage continued to increase and spread across the tissue for approximately 6 hr (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: FM 1-43 is commonly used to label damaged cell membranes after wounding.
source: To label wounded epithelium, we used the lipophilic dye FM 1–43, which is commonly used to label damaged cell membranes after wounding (Defour et al., 2014; Sønder et al., 2022; McDade et al., 2021; Shannon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Immediately following either transection or thermal injury, axonal damage overlaps spatially with wounded epithelial tissue.
source: Immediately following either transection or thermal injury, axonal damage overlapped spatially with wounded epithelial tissue (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by FM 1-43 and GCaMP5 co-labeling data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: By 6 hours following burn injury, there is widespread damage to axons that extends beyond the initial wound area.
source: However, by 6 hr following burn injury, there was widespread damage to axons that extended beyond the initial wound area (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by FM 1-43 and GCaMP5 co-labeling data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Burn injury induces axonal damage that accumulates over time and is spatially uncoupled from the surrounding epithelial damage.
source: These findings suggest that burn injury induces axonal damage that accumulates over time and is spatially uncoupled from the surrounding epithelial damage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that axonal damage spreads beyond the area of epithelial damage over time.

claim: Larvae that underwent only transections at both time points had full sensory function by 24 hours post-wound regardless of the timing of the second transection injury.
source: As expected, larvae that underwent only transections at both time points had full sensory function by 24 hpw regardless of the timing of the second transection injury, showing that zebrafish efficiently heal after mechanical damage (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Zebrafish efficiently heal after mechanical damage.
source: As expected, larvae that underwent only transections at both time points had full sensory function by 24 hpw regardless of the timing of the second transection injury, showing that zebrafish efficiently heal after mechanical damage (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that repeated transections do not impair sensory function recovery.

claim: Early transection after thermal injury (5 minutes post-wound) improves sensory axon regeneration and function to levels similar to transected larvae.
source: In burned larvae, early transection after thermal injury (5 mpw) improved sensory axon regeneration and function to levels similar to transected larvae (Figure 2C–E), suggesting that burn injury does not immediately affect sensory axons differently than mechanical damage.
evidence: Supported by axon density and touch assay data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Burn injury does not immediately affect sensory axons differently than mechanical damage.
source: In burned larvae, early transection after thermal injury (5 mpw) improved sensory axon regeneration and function to levels similar to transected larvae (Figure 2C–E), suggesting that burn injury does not immediately affect sensory axons differently than mechanical damage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that early removal of burned tissue rescues sensory function.

claim: When burned tissue is excised after 6 hours, significant defects are noted in both axon density and sensory function compared to larvae that received two transection injuries.
source: However, when burned tissue was excised after 6 hr, significant defects were noted in both axon density and sensory function compared to larvae that either received two transection injuries or had burned tissue transected at 5 mpw (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by axon density and touch assay data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: When burned tissue is excised after 6 hours, significant defects are noted in both axon density and sensory function compared to larvae that had burned tissue transected at 5 minutes post-wound.
source: However, when burned tissue was excised after 6 hr, significant defects were noted in both axon density and sensory function compared to larvae that either received two transection injuries or had burned tissue transected at 5 mpw (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by axon density and touch assay data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The local wound environment modulates sensory axon outcomes following burn injury.
source: These findings suggest that the local wound environment modulates sensory axon outcomes following burn injury, and that events in the first 6 hr after injury impact longer-term sensory axon repair.
evidence: Inferred from the two-wound experiment results showing that timing of tissue removal affects outcomes.

claim: Events in the first 6 hours after burn injury impact longer-term sensory axon repair.
source: These findings suggest that the local wound environment modulates sensory axon outcomes following burn injury, and that events in the first 6 hr after injury impact longer-term sensory axon repair.
evidence: Inferred from the two-wound experiment results showing that early vs. late tissue removal has different outcomes.

claim: The axons of sensory neurons are ensheathed within actin-rich channels running through basal keratinocytes.
source: The axons of sensory neurons are ensheathed within actin-rich channels running through basal keratinocytes (O'Brien et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In response to transection, keratinocytes distal to the wound edge remain relatively stationary.
source: In response to transection, we initially observed characteristic epithelial cell contraction at the wound edge; however, keratinocytes distal to the wound edge remained relatively stationary (Figure 3A; Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 1.

claim: Burn wounding results in a rapid collective movement of keratinocytes toward the site of tissue damage.
source: In contrast, burn wounding resulted in a rapid collective movement of keratinocytes toward the site of tissue damage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Basal keratinocytes move an average total distance of 205.7±10.7 µm in the first hour following burn injury.
source: Live-imaging experiments revealed that basal keratinocytes, on average, moved a total distance of 205.7±10.7 µm in the first hour following burn injury, which was significantly greater than the 58.9±5.8 µm of migration observed following tailfin transection (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Basal keratinocytes move an average total distance of 58.9±5.8 µm in the first hour following tailfin transection.
source: Live-imaging experiments revealed that basal keratinocytes, on average, moved a total distance of 205.7±10.7 µm in the first hour following burn injury, which was significantly greater than the 58.9±5.8 µm of migration observed following tailfin transection (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Keratinocyte movement after burn injury is significantly greater than after tailfin transection.
source: Live-imaging experiments revealed that basal keratinocytes, on average, moved a total distance of 205.7±10.7 µm in the first hour following burn injury, which was significantly greater than the 58.9±5.8 µm of migration observed following tailfin transection (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of cell tracking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Keratinocytes move as a collective in response to burn injury but exhibit chaotic movement.
source: Although keratinocytes moved as a collective in response to burn injury, they exhibited chaotic movement and appeared to be loosely associated with their neighbors.
evidence: Supported by qualitative observations from live imaging data.

claim: Keratinocytes after burn injury appear to be loosely associated with their neighbors.
source: Although keratinocytes moved as a collective in response to burn injury, they exhibited chaotic movement and appeared to be loosely associated with their neighbors.
evidence: Supported by qualitative observations from live imaging data.

claim: Unwounded larvae have regularly shaped keratinocytes with even actin distribution around the cell periphery in both the superficial and basal layers.
source: Unwounded larvae had regularly shaped keratinocytes with even actin distribution around the cell periphery in both the superficial and basal layers (Figure 3C), indicative of a non-migratory epithelium.
evidence: Supported by Lifeact imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Regular keratinocyte shape with even actin distribution is indicative of a non-migratory epithelium.
source: Unwounded larvae had regularly shaped keratinocytes with even actin distribution around the cell periphery in both the superficial and basal layers (Figure 3C), indicative of a non-migratory epithelium.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cell morphology and migration.

claim: Superficial keratinocytes in burned larvae are elongated and have an even actin distribution.
source: Superficial keratinocytes in burned larvae were elongated and had an even actin distribution, but the basal keratinocytes showed actin localization to the leading edge with the formation of lamellipodia (Figure 3C), suggesting that the superficial keratinocytes are being pulled by the motile basal keratinocytes.
evidence: Supported by Lifeact imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Basal keratinocytes in burned larvae show actin localization to the leading edge with the formation of lamellipodia.
source: Superficial keratinocytes in burned larvae were elongated and had an even actin distribution, but the basal keratinocytes showed actin localization to the leading edge with the formation of lamellipodia (Figure 3C), suggesting that the superficial keratinocytes are being pulled by the motile basal keratinocytes.
evidence: Supported by Lifeact imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Superficial keratinocytes are being pulled by the motile basal keratinocytes after burn injury.
source: Superficial keratinocytes in burned larvae were elongated and had an even actin distribution, but the basal keratinocytes showed actin localization to the leading edge with the formation of lamellipodia (Figure 3C), suggesting that the superficial keratinocytes are being pulled by the motile basal keratinocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the morphological differences between superficial and basal keratinocytes.

claim: Sensory axon movement is coordinated with keratinocyte migration following thermal injury.
source: Simultaneous imaging of basal keratinocytes and sensory axons following thermal injury revealed that sensory axon movement is coordinated with keratinocyte migration (Figure 3D; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by dual-labeled imaging data shown in Figure 3D and Video 2.

claim: Within the first hour after burn, calcium-positive punctae coincide with keratinocyte migration.
source: Within the first hour after burn, calcium-positive punctae were identified that coincided with keratinocyte migration, indicating that early keratinocyte migration was associated with the initial axonal damage (Video 3).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Video 3.

claim: Early keratinocyte migration is associated with the initial axonal damage after burn injury.
source: Within the first hour after burn, calcium-positive punctae were identified that coincided with keratinocyte migration, indicating that early keratinocyte migration was associated with the initial axonal damage (Video 3).
evidence: Inferred from the temporal and spatial coincidence of keratinocyte migration and axonal damage.

claim: At 3 days post-fertilization, the skin is innervated by Rohon-Beard (RB) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons.
source: At 3 dpf, the skin is innervated by Rohon-Beard (RB) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons with cell bodies that reside within and just outside the spinal cord, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of zebrafish neuroanatomy.

claim: RB neuron cell bodies reside within the spinal cord.
source: At 3 dpf, the skin is innervated by Rohon-Beard (RB) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons with cell bodies that reside within and just outside the spinal cord, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of zebrafish neuroanatomy.

claim: DRG neuron cell bodies reside just outside the spinal cord.
source: At 3 dpf, the skin is innervated by Rohon-Beard (RB) and dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons with cell bodies that reside within and just outside the spinal cord, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of zebrafish neuroanatomy.

claim: Both the RB and DRG cell bodies that innervate the caudal fin are intact and non-motile following burn injury.
source: Following burn injury, we noted that both the RB and DRG cell bodies that innervate the caudal fin were intact and non-motile in comparison to their pre-burn morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Sensory axons are displaced along with the collective movement of basal keratinocytes following burn.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that sensory axons are displaced along with the collective movement of basal keratinocytes following burn, and that this early movement is associated with the start of axonal damage.
evidence: Inferred from the coordinated movement of axons and keratinocytes observed in imaging data.

claim: Early keratinocyte movement following burn is associated with the start of axonal damage.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that sensory axons are displaced along with the collective movement of basal keratinocytes following burn, and that this early movement is associated with the start of axonal damage.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal coincidence of keratinocyte migration and axonal damage onset.

claim: Arp2/3 is a known regulator of leading-edge actin dynamics and migration.
source: We next determined if a known regulator of leading-edge actin dynamics and migration, Arp2/3, modulates the movement of basal keratinocytes after burn (Henson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 limits keratinocyte lamellipodia formation after burn injury.
source: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 limited keratinocyte lamellipodia formation and impaired early keratinocyte migration, indicating that the early keratinocyte movement is Arp2/3 dependent (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by Lifeact imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 impairs early keratinocyte migration after burn injury.
source: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 limited keratinocyte lamellipodia formation and impaired early keratinocyte migration, indicating that the early keratinocyte movement is Arp2/3 dependent (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Early keratinocyte movement after burn is Arp2/3 dependent.
source: Treatment with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK666 limited keratinocyte lamellipodia formation and impaired early keratinocyte migration, indicating that the early keratinocyte movement is Arp2/3 dependent (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Inferred from the effect of CK666 treatment on keratinocyte migration.

claim: By 40 minutes post-wound, keratinocyte migration is not significantly different between control and CK666-treated larvae.
source: Although early migration was impaired, by 40 mpw the migration was not significantly different between control and CK666-treated larvae, suggesting that CK666 treatment only inhibits early keratinocyte migration.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data over time.

claim: CK666 treatment only inhibits early keratinocyte migration.
source: Although early migration was impaired, by 40 mpw the migration was not significantly different between control and CK666-treated larvae, suggesting that CK666 treatment only inhibits early keratinocyte migration.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal pattern of CK666 effects on migration.

claim: Efficient tissue repair after injury relies on coordinated ROS production by epithelial cells.
source: It is known that efficient tissue repair after injury relies on coordinated ROS production by epithelial cells (Enyedi and Niethammer, 2015; Jelcic et al., 2019; Yoo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Following mechanical injuries such as tailfin transection or laser ablation, transient and localized H2O2 promotes sensory axon regeneration and wound healing.
source: Following mechanical injuries such as tailfin transection or laser ablation, transient and localized H2O2 also promotes sensory axon regeneration and wound healing (Cadiz Diaz et al., 2022; Rieger and Sagasti, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Early after burn wounding, there is robust generation of hydrogen peroxide in burned tissue.
source: Early after burn wounding, there was robust generation of hydrogen peroxide in burned tissue that was dampened in CK666-treated larvae.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf fluorescence measurements.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide generation after burn is dampened in CK666-treated larvae.
source: Early after burn wounding, there was robust generation of hydrogen peroxide in burned tissue that was dampened in CK666-treated larvae.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: In the presence of CK666, H2O2 production is concentrated at the wound edge, similar to tail transection.
source: In the presence of CK666, H2O2 production was concentrated at the wound edge, similar to what has been reported with tail transection (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4D-E and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Early migration alters the temporal and spatial distribution of ROS after wounding.
source: These findings suggest that early migration alters the temporal and spatial distribution of ROS after wounding.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of CK666 on ROS distribution.

claim: CK666-treated larvae have no significant difference in axon damage 24 hours after burn compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, CK666-treated larvae had no significant difference in axon damage or regeneration 24 hr after burn compared to controls, although there was a trend toward improved sensory function (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CK666-treated larvae have no significant difference in axon regeneration 24 hours after burn compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, CK666-treated larvae had no significant difference in axon damage or regeneration 24 hr after burn compared to controls, although there was a trend toward improved sensory function (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CK666-treated larvae show a trend toward improved sensory function 24 hours after burn.
source: Interestingly, CK666-treated larvae had no significant difference in axon damage or regeneration 24 hr after burn compared to controls, although there was a trend toward improved sensory function (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Keratinocyte migration regulates early tissue scale ROS production after burn injury.
source: Taken together, the findings suggest that keratinocyte migration regulates early tissue scale ROS production after burn injury.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of inhibiting migration on ROS distribution.

claim: The presence of an osmotic gradient promotes keratinocyte migration via cell swelling in response to mechanical injury.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the presence of an osmotic gradient promotes keratinocyte migration via cell swelling in response to mechanical injury (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Removing the osmotic gradient by wounding larvae in isotonic solution inhibits keratinocyte migration following mechanical injury.
source: Removing this osmotic gradient by wounding larvae in the presence of solution that is isotonic to the interstitial fluid has previously been shown to inhibit keratinocyte migration following mechanical injury and impair wound healing (Gault et al., 2014; Kennard and Theriot, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wounding in isotonic solution impairs wound healing after mechanical injury.
source: Removing this osmotic gradient by wounding larvae in the presence of solution that is isotonic to the interstitial fluid has previously been shown to inhibit keratinocyte migration following mechanical injury and impair wound healing (Gault et al., 2014; Kennard and Theriot, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wounding in the presence of isotonic solution prevents the rapid movement of keratinocytes in response to a burn.
source: We found that wounding in the presence of an isotonic solution prevented the rapid movement of keratinocytes in response to a burn.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Within the first hour following burn injury, keratinocyte average speed is reduced from 0.059 µm/s in control medium to 0.003 µm/s in isotonic medium.
source: Within the first hour following burn injury, keratinocyte average speed was reduced from 0.059 µm/s in control medium to 0.003 µm/s in isotonic medium (Figure 5A–C; Video 4).
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immediately following burn injury, the level of H2O2 is the same between control and isotonic treatment groups.
source: Immediately following burn injury, the level of H2O2 was the same between the treatment groups, indicating that cells wounded in the presence of isotonic solution maintain their normal ability to generate ROS (Figure 5F and G; Enyedi and Niethammer, 2015).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5G and citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells wounded in the presence of isotonic solution maintain their normal ability to generate ROS.
source: Immediately following burn injury, the level of H2O2 was the same between the treatment groups, indicating that cells wounded in the presence of isotonic solution maintain their normal ability to generate ROS (Figure 5F and G; Enyedi and Niethammer, 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that initial ROS levels are similar between treatments.

claim: During the first hour post-burn, control larvae have increased ROS throughout the fin tissue compared to isotonic-treated larvae.
source: Examining ROS production during the first hour post-burn revealed that control larvae had increased ROS throughout the fin tissue compared to isotonic-treated larvae, while both conditions had comparable levels of ROS at the wound (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: During the first hour post-burn, both control and isotonic-treated larvae have comparable levels of ROS at the wound.
source: Examining ROS production during the first hour post-burn revealed that control larvae had increased ROS throughout the fin tissue compared to isotonic-treated larvae, while both conditions had comparable levels of ROS at the wound (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: At 6 hours post-burn, H2O2 production is no longer localized to the wound edge in control burned larvae and has increased throughout the tailfin.
source: At 6 hr post-burn, H2O2 production was no longer localized to the wound edge in control burned larvae and had increased throughout the tailfin.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5F and H.

claim: At 6 hours post-burn, H2O2 remains restricted to the wound edge in larvae burned in the presence of isotonic solution.
source: By contrast, H2O2 remained restricted to the wound edge in larvae burned in the presence of isotonic solution, displaying a similar localized pattern to that observed after mechanical injury (Figure 5F; Jelcic et al., 2019; Korte et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5F and H, and citations to prior literature.

claim: H2O2 level at the wound edge is similar between control and isotonic-treated larvae 6 hours post-wound.
source: Quantification revealed that H2O2 level at the wound edge was similar between control and isotonic-treated larvae 6 hpw.
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The level of H2O2 is approximately sixfold lower in the fin epithelial tissue adjacent to the burn wound with isotonic treatment at 6 hours post-wound.
source: However, the level of H2O2 was approximately sixfold lower in the fin epithelial tissue adjacent to the burn wound with isotonic treatment (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Robust keratinocyte movement induced by burn injury generates an oxidative environment at the tissue scale.
source: These findings suggest that robust keratinocyte movement induced by burn injury generates an oxidative environment at the tissue scale.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between keratinocyte migration and tissue-scale ROS production.

claim: Immediately following injury, larvae burned in isotonic solution display axon damage similar to larvae injured in control medium.
source: Immediately following injury, larvae burned in isotonic solution displayed axon damage similar to larvae injured in control medium (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 6 hours post-wound, axonal damage in isotonic-treated larvae is reduced and remains restricted to the site of injury.
source: However, 6 hpw, axonal damage in isotonic-treated larvae was reduced and remained restricted to the site of injury, similar to the spatially restricted H2O2 signal induced by isotonic treatment (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Larvae burned in isotonic medium have significantly greater axon density at 24 hours post-wound.
source: Accordingly, larvae burned in isotonic medium had significantly greater axon density 24 hpw, and more than 85% of isotonic-treated larvae had normal sensory function by 24 hpw (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: More than 85% of isotonic-treated larvae have normal sensory function by 24 hours post-wound.
source: Accordingly, larvae burned in isotonic medium had significantly greater axon density 24 hpw, and more than 85% of isotonic-treated larvae had normal sensory function by 24 hpw (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: An isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol limits basal keratinocyte migration after burn injury.
source: We also found that an isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol limited basal keratinocyte migration and had normal axon density and sensory function 24 hpw, suggesting that the benefit of isotonic solution is independent of effects on electrical cues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: An isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol results in normal axon density 24 hours post-wound after burn injury.
source: We also found that an isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol limited basal keratinocyte migration and had normal axon density and sensory function 24 hpw, suggesting that the benefit of isotonic solution is independent of effects on electrical cues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: An isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol results in normal sensory function 24 hours post-wound after burn injury.
source: We also found that an isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol limited basal keratinocyte migration and had normal axon density and sensory function 24 hpw, suggesting that the benefit of isotonic solution is independent of effects on electrical cues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The benefit of isotonic solution is independent of effects on electrical cues.
source: We also found that an isotonic solution with D-Sorbitol limited basal keratinocyte migration and had normal axon density and sensory function 24 hpw, suggesting that the benefit of isotonic solution is independent of effects on electrical cues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Inferred from the similar effects of NaCl and D-Sorbitol isotonic solutions.

claim: When isotonic medium is added 1 hour post-wound, there is no rescue of ROS production in either the wound area or the fin at 6 hours post-wound.
source: When isotonic medium was added 1 hpw, after keratinocyte migration was complete, there was no rescue of ROS production in either the wound area or the fin 6 hpw (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by Pfbsf measurements shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: When isotonic treatment starts 1 hour post-wound, there is no improvement in sensory axon density at 24 hours post-wound.
source: Additionally, there was no improvement in sensory axon density or function 24 hpw, supporting the idea that early wound events during the first hour are critical for their effects on later sensory neuron function (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements shown in Figure 6J.

claim: When isotonic treatment starts 1 hour post-wound, there is no improvement in sensory function at 24 hours post-wound.
source: Additionally, there was no improvement in sensory axon density or function 24 hpw, supporting the idea that early wound events during the first hour are critical for their effects on later sensory neuron function (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: Supported by touch assay data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Early wound events during the first hour are critical for their effects on later sensory neuron function.
source: Additionally, there was no improvement in sensory axon density or function 24 hpw, supporting the idea that early wound events during the first hour are critical for their effects on later sensory neuron function (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: Inferred from the timing-dependent effects of isotonic treatment.

claim: Early keratinocyte movement after burn coordinates spatial redox signaling and impacts sensory axon regeneration.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that early keratinocyte movement after burn coordinates spatial redox signaling and impacts sensory axon regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental findings showing that early keratinocyte migration affects ROS distribution and sensory neuron outcomes.

claim: Collective keratinocyte migration is conserved across species.
source: Collective keratinocyte migration is conserved across species and is required to mediate wound closure after tissue injury (Kirfel and Herzog, 2004; Mayor and Etienne-Manneville, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Collective keratinocyte migration is required to mediate wound closure after tissue injury.
source: Collective keratinocyte migration is conserved across species and is required to mediate wound closure after tissue injury (Kirfel and Herzog, 2004; Mayor and Etienne-Manneville, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Excessive keratinocyte migration is a defining feature of the response to burn injury.
source: In comparison to the organized movement associated with keratinocyte response to mechanical injury, our observations here identify excessive keratinocyte migration as a defining feature of the response to burn injury.
evidence: Supported by the experimental observations of keratinocyte behavior after burn vs. transection.

claim: Basal keratinocyte migration following burn injury lacks a stereotypical leader-follower dynamic.
source: Basal keratinocyte migration following burn injury appeared to lack a stereotypical leader-follower dynamic, with cells instead moving independently of one another but as a collective group.
evidence: Supported by qualitative observations from live imaging data.

claim: Collective keratinocyte migration is a feature of tissue repair in larval zebrafish regardless of the mode of injury.
source: This observation suggests that collective keratinocyte migration is a feature of tissue repair in larval zebrafish regardless of the mode of injury and that its regulation is required for the success of long-term healing.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of collective migration in both burn and transection injuries.

claim: Regulation of collective keratinocyte migration is required for the success of long-term healing.
source: This observation suggests that collective keratinocyte migration is a feature of tissue repair in larval zebrafish regardless of the mode of injury and that its regulation is required for the success of long-term healing.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing that dysregulated migration impairs healing.

claim: Early migration and formation of lamellipodia in basal keratinocytes requires Arp2/3 signaling.
source: Indeed, we provide evidence that early migration and formation of lamellipodia in basal keratinocytes requires Arp2/3 signaling, and that this aberrant migration regulates the temporal and spatial distribution of early redox signaling in the wound tissue.
evidence: Supported by CK666 inhibition experiments.

claim: Aberrant keratinocyte migration regulates the temporal and spatial distribution of early redox signaling in the wound tissue.
source: Indeed, we provide evidence that early migration and formation of lamellipodia in basal keratinocytes requires Arp2/3 signaling, and that this aberrant migration regulates the temporal and spatial distribution of early redox signaling in the wound tissue.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing that inhibiting migration alters ROS distribution.

claim: Arp2/3 inhibition does not lead to sustained control of keratinocyte migration.
source: However, Arp2/3 inhibition did not lead to sustained control of keratinocyte migration and production of ROS eventually increased throughout the tailfin.
evidence: Supported by time-course data showing recovery of migration after initial inhibition.

claim: Production of ROS eventually increases throughout the tailfin after Arp2/3 inhibition.
source: However, Arp2/3 inhibition did not lead to sustained control of keratinocyte migration and production of ROS eventually increased throughout the tailfin.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurements over time in CK666-treated larvae.

claim: Sensory function is not significantly improved at 24 hours post-wound with Arp2/3 inhibition.
source: Accordingly, sensory function was not significantly improved at 24 hpw.
evidence: Supported by touch assay data in CK666-treated larvae.

claim: Osmotic treatment affects basal keratinocyte motility in response to burn injury.
source: Our results also show that osmotic modulation affects basal keratinocyte motility in response to burn injury.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: Limiting keratinocyte motility by isotonic treatment is detrimental to tissue repair following mechanical injury.
source: Interestingly, limiting keratinocyte motility by isotonic treatment is detrimental to tissue repair following mechanical injury (Gault et al., 2014), but isotonic treatment both rescues epithelial morphology and reduces axon damage following thermal injury.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Isotonic treatment rescues epithelial morphology following thermal injury.
source: Interestingly, limiting keratinocyte motility by isotonic treatment is detrimental to tissue repair following mechanical injury (Gault et al., 2014), but isotonic treatment both rescues epithelial morphology and reduces axon damage following thermal injury.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in this study.

claim: Isotonic treatment reduces axon damage following thermal injury.
source: Interestingly, limiting keratinocyte motility by isotonic treatment is detrimental to tissue repair following mechanical injury (Gault et al., 2014), but isotonic treatment both rescues epithelial morphology and reduces axon damage following thermal injury.
evidence: Supported by GCaMP5 imaging data in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: There is an optimal amount of keratinocyte movement needed for efficient repair and long-term regeneration.
source: This suggests that there is an optimal amount of keratinocyte movement needed for efficient repair and long-term regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting effects of isotonic treatment on mechanical vs. thermal injury.

claim: ROS signaling provides a framework to understand how early wound-induced events are linked to long-term repair.
source: ROS signaling provides a framework to understand this link due to its requirement for both early wound contraction and long-term regeneration.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ROS roles in wound healing.

claim: In zebrafish, H2O2 is generated along a tissue scale gradient with the highest levels at the wound edge.
source: In zebrafish, the ROS H2O2 is generated along a tissue scale gradient with the highest levels at the wound edge (Niethammer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Uncontrolled ROS production is damaging to tissues.
source: While this spatial gradient undoubtedly directs cell function based on the position along the gradient, uncontrolled ROS production is damaging to tissues.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: A mechanism must exist to control ROS such that it remains relatively localized to the site of damage and is controlled temporally and spatially.
source: Therefore, a mechanism must exist to control ROS such that it remains relatively localized to the site of damage and is controlled temporally and spatially.
evidence: Inferred from the need to balance beneficial and harmful effects of ROS.

claim: Keratinocyte redox signaling is critical for long-term repair.
source: In addition to their early role in wound resealing, keratinocyte redox signaling is critical for long-term repair.
evidence: Based on established knowledge and experimental findings.

claim: Cell swelling induces cPLA2-dependent 5-oxoETE production and immune cell recruitment.
source: Cell swelling induces cPLA2-dependent 5-oxoETE production and immune cell recruitment (Enyedi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The signals that control keratinocyte motility may simultaneously modify long-term keratinocyte signaling.
source: This suggests the signals that control keratinocyte motility may simultaneously modify long-term keratinocyte signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the connection between cell swelling, migration, and signaling.

claim: Cell migration can modulate tissue scale signaling following injury.
source: Our findings suggest that cell migration can modulate tissue scale signaling following injury.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing that migration affects ROS distribution.

claim: Isotonic treatment blocks keratinocyte movement and restores localized ROS signaling at the wound edge.
source: Importantly, isotonic treatment blocks keratinocyte movement and restores localized ROS signaling at the wound edge.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking and ROS measurements in isotonic-treated larvae.

claim: The dependence of ROS distribution on migration is supported by the effects of Arp2/3 inhibition on early ROS signaling.
source: The dependence on migration was supported both by the effects of Arp2/3 inhibition on early ROS signaling and by the finding that isotonic treatment started after migration was complete (1 hr after injury) did not rescue tissue scale ROS.
evidence: Supported by CK666 experiments showing altered ROS distribution.

claim: Isotonic treatment started after migration is complete (1 hour after injury) does not rescue tissue scale ROS.
source: The dependence on migration was supported both by the effects of Arp2/3 inhibition on early ROS signaling and by the finding that isotonic treatment started after migration was complete (1 hr after injury) did not rescue tissue scale ROS.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurements in larvae treated with isotonic solution at 1 hour post-wound.

claim: Early keratinocyte migration patterns the tissue scale ROS distribution.
source: This suggests that early keratinocyte migration patterns the tissue scale ROS distribution.
evidence: Inferred from the timing-dependent effects of migration inhibition on ROS distribution.

claim: ROS inhibition with DPI provides only slight benefits to axon regeneration.
source: Additionally, ROS inhibition with the drug DPI provided only slight benefits to axon regeneration.
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements in DPI-treated larvae.

claim: Isotonic treatment at the time of injury is sufficient to rescue sensory function.
source: The finding that isotonic treatment at the time of injury was sufficient to rescue sensory function but treatment after 1 hr did not rescue axon regeneration further highlights the importance of this early motile response for setting up the longer-term repair after damage.
evidence: Supported by touch assay data comparing timing of isotonic treatment.

claim: Isotonic treatment after 1 hour does not rescue axon regeneration.
source: The finding that isotonic treatment at the time of injury was sufficient to rescue sensory function but treatment after 1 hr did not rescue axon regeneration further highlights the importance of this early motile response for setting up the longer-term repair after damage.
evidence: Supported by axon density measurements comparing timing of isotonic treatment.

claim: The early motile response is important for setting up the longer-term repair after damage.
source: The finding that isotonic treatment at the time of injury was sufficient to rescue sensory function but treatment after 1 hr did not rescue axon regeneration further highlights the importance of this early motile response for setting up the longer-term repair after damage.
evidence: Inferred from the timing-dependent effects of isotonic treatment.

claim: A system in which keratinocyte motility controls downstream signaling enables signaling to be scaled to the size of injury.
source: The benefit of a system in which keratinocyte motility controls downstream signaling is twofold. First, it enables signaling to be scaled to the size of injury.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional benefits of the observed mechanism.

claim: If more cells migrate due to a larger injury, then production of ROS will likewise increase.
source: If more cells migrate due to a larger injury, then production of ROS will likewise increase.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about how the mechanism would scale with injury size.

claim: A system in which keratinocyte motility controls downstream signaling provides a mechanism to control the spatial localization of signaling.
source: Second, this system provides a mechanism to control the spatial localization of signaling.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the functional benefits of the observed mechanism.

claim: Keratinocyte migration requires transiently detaching from neighboring cells.
source: Keratinocyte migration requires transiently detaching from neighboring cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cell migration mechanisms.

claim: The act of migrating induces a physical change in the tissue that demarcates the wound region from healthy tissue.
source: Thus, the act of migrating induces a physical change in the tissue that demarcates the wound region from healthy tissue.
evidence: Inferred from the physical changes associated with cell migration.

claim: Production of ROS promotes keratinocyte motility.
source: It is known that production of ROS promotes keratinocyte motility, and that adhesion is linked to cellular redox state (Dunnill et al., 2017; Mendieta-Serrano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adhesion is linked to cellular redox state.
source: It is known that production of ROS promotes keratinocyte motility, and that adhesion is linked to cellular redox state (Dunnill et al., 2017; Mendieta-Serrano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ROS production in wounded tissue may be linked to the biomechanical state of keratinocytes.
source: Given these observations, it seems plausible that ROS production in wounded tissue is linked to the biomechanical state of keratinocytes – with low ROS in static, adhered cells, and high ROS in loosely adhered or migrating cells.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed relationships between migration, adhesion, and ROS.

claim: A conceptual framework linking ROS production to keratinocyte biomechanical state would explain excessive ROS production in burn wounded tissue.
source: A conceptual framework such as this would explain excessive ROS production in burn wounded tissue.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about how the proposed mechanism explains the observations.

claim: Early keratinocyte dynamics in burned tissue are associated with normal wound edge ROS production.
source: Early keratinocyte dynamics in burned tissue are associated with normal wound edge ROS production.
evidence: Supported by ROS measurements showing similar initial wound edge ROS in burn and transection.

claim: Lack of a migratory stop signal may result in excessive keratinocyte migration after burn injury.
source: However, lack of a migratory stop signal may result in excessive keratinocyte migration and subsequent epithelial damage associated with keratinocytes detaching from the basal lamina.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying excessive migration.

claim: Excessive keratinocyte migration may result in subsequent epithelial damage associated with keratinocytes detaching from the basal lamina.
source: However, lack of a migratory stop signal may result in excessive keratinocyte migration and subsequent epithelial damage associated with keratinocytes detaching from the basal lamina.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the consequences of excessive migration.

claim: Failure to restore epithelial homeostasis due to unabated keratinocyte movement may allow for ROS production to continue over time and spread further away from the wound site.
source: Therefore, failure to restore epithelial homeostasis due to unabated keratinocyte movement may allow for ROS production to continue over time and spread further away from the wound site.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the mechanism linking sustained migration to prolonged ROS production.

claim: Early wound-induced keratinocyte migration is a mechanism that controls spatial patterning of long-term wound signaling.
source: In summary, we have identified early wound-induced keratinocyte migration as a mechanism that controls spatial patterning of long-term wound signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental findings.

claim: Keratinocytes within the wound microenvironment can integrate early signaling and migratory functions that mediate initial wound closure.
source: These findings highlight the ability of keratinocytes within the wound microenvironment to integrate early signaling and migratory functions that mediate initial wound closure and subsequently regulate spatial tissue signaling necessary for efficient repair of sensory neuron function.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing keratinocyte roles in both migration and signaling.

claim: Keratinocytes subsequently regulate spatial tissue signaling necessary for efficient repair of sensory neuron function.
source: These findings highlight the ability of keratinocytes within the wound microenvironment to integrate early signaling and migratory functions that mediate initial wound closure and subsequently regulate spatial tissue signaling necessary for efficient repair of sensory neuron function.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings showing that keratinocyte behavior affects sensory neuron outcomes.

claim: Larval zebrafish are useful for revealing new insights of the tissue response to injury in vivo.
source: Further, our results not only highlight the utility of larval zebrafish for revealing new insights of the tissue response to injury in vivo, but also demonstrate the potential for these findings to inform new treatment strategies for wound healing more broadly.
evidence: Based on the successful use of zebrafish in this study.

claim: These findings have the potential to inform new treatment strategies for wound healing more broadly.
source: Further, our results not only highlight the utility of larval zebrafish for revealing new insights of the tissue response to injury in vivo, but also demonstrate the potential for these findings to inform new treatment strategies for wound healing more broadly.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the translational potential of the findings.

claim: Larval zebrafish caudal fins can regenerate fully by 3 days post-transection.
source: Larval zebrafish caudal fins can regenerate fully by 3 days post-transection, with 60% of fin regrowth occurring by day 1.5 (Lisse et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: 60% of larval zebrafish fin regrowth occurs by day 1.5 post-transection.
source: Larval zebrafish caudal fins can regenerate fully by 3 days post-transection, with 60% of fin regrowth occurring by day 1.5 (Lisse et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.
